meta.title: Who really said "Fortune favors the bold"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Virgil really wrote the line (Aeneid 10.284, spoken by Turnus) — but it was an old Roman proverb he echoed, and the English saying predates any Virgil translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Fortune favors the bold'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's a real Virgil line — but he didn't coin it. The idea was an old Roman proverb, and the English phrase goes back to Chaucer and Gower.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 70–19 BC · Roman poet, author of the Aeneid
answer.sourceLine: The line ‘audentis Fortuna iuvat’ ↗ is genuinely Virgil’s — Aeneid Book 10, line 284, shouted by the Rutulian prince Turnus as he rallies his men against the landing Trojans — and the “bold/daring” wording tracks Virgil’s audentis specifically. But Virgil did not coin the thought: it was already a stock Roman proverb (used earlier by Ennius and Terence, and called an ‘old proverb’ by Cicero ↗), and the English saying stands on its own, attested centuries before any English Aeneid.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Turnus, the Rutulian prince — Aeneas’s enemy

source.excerpt: Turnus, seeing the Trojans come ashore, spurs his warriors on: “audentis Fortuna iuvat” — “Fortune favours the daring.” The irony is that Turnus is the poem’s antagonist, and Fortune does not save him: he is killed by Aeneas in the final lines.
trail: The Latin ‘audentis Fortuna iuvat’ sits at Aeneid 10.284 and is spoken by Turnus ↗, not by Virgil in his own voice.
The sentiment predates Virgil: Terence used ‘fortis Fortuna adiuvat’ in the Phormio (line 203), and Cicero already called it an old proverb ↗.
The English saying is older than any English Virgil: it appears in Chaucer (c. 1385) and Gower’s ‘Fortune unto the bolde Is favorable’ (c. 1390) ↗.
Only some translators land on this exact wording — David West (1990) renders it ‘Fortune favors the bold’, while Dryden (1697) had ‘Fortune befriends the bold’ ↗.
source.excerptNote: Latin as printed in standard critical editions of the Aeneid; the archaic accusative plural audentis is often modernised to audentes.

sourceLink.text: Translation chronology for Aeneid 10.284, Ogilby (1649) to Fagles (2006)

source.rightsNote: The displayed English wording is a centuries-old proverb — attested in Chaucer (c. 1385) and Gower (c. 1390) ↗, far earlier than 1931 — and the underlying Latin of Virgil, Terence and Ennius is ancient; both are public domain. Note that a specific modern translation of the Aeneid (e.g. David West’s 1990 Penguin text, which reads “Fortune favors the bold”) carries its own copyright, but the free-standing proverb shown here does not.

author.name: Virgil
author.heading: About Virgil
author.metaLine: 70–19 BC · Roman poet, author of the Aeneid
author.bio: Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC) was ancient Rome’s foremost poet, author of the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the national epic the Aeneid. The Aeneid, composed over the last decade of his life and left unfinished at his death, follows the Trojan hero Aeneas to Italy and became the central text of the Latin canon. Virgil frequently wove existing Roman proverbs and religious formulae into his verse — as here, where he gives an old saying about Fortune to the doomed warrior Turnus.

cite.sourceCitation: Virgil, Aeneid 10.284 (“audentis Fortuna iuvat”), composed c. 29–19 BC; cf. Terence, Phormio 203, and Ennius, Annals 257. English proverb attested from Chaucer, Troilus & Criseyde (c. 1385) and Gower, Confessio Amantis (c. 1390).

misattribution.heading: Misquote & misattribution
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Virgil is not wrong — the line really is in the Aeneid — but two things are usually lost: Virgil didn’t originate the idea, and the popular English phrase is a proverb in its own right, not a quotation lifted from Virgil.

items.why: The thought was already proverbial in Rome. Terence used ‘fortis Fortuna adiuvat’ in the Phormio (line 203), and Cicero cited it as a vetus proverbium ↗; the proverb dictionaries trace it back to Ennius, Annals 257 ↗.

items.who: An old English proverb, not a line quoted from Virgil
items.why: It is attested in English in Chaucer’s Troilus & Criseyde (c. 1385) and Gower’s Confessio Amantis (c. 1390) ↗ — centuries before any English translation of the Aeneid — so the saying you know is not a rendering of Virgil so much as a parallel proverb.

items.who: Two Latin lines, two English sayings
items.why: ‘Fortune favours the bold’ matches Virgil’s audentis (daring), while ‘fortune favours the brave’ matches Terence’s fortes (strong/brave) ↗ — which is why the two English versions are both ‘right’ but point at different ancient sources.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: Virgil really wrote ‘audentis Fortuna iuvat’ at Aeneid 10.284 ↗, and it is a fair source for “Fortune favours the bold” — but he was quoting a proverb that was old even in his day, and the English saying has its own independent life.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Part of the phrase’s appeal is dramatic irony. In the Aeneid it is not the hero who says it but Turnus, Aeneas’s doomed rival, urging his men into a battle he will ultimately lose — Fortune, in the poem, does not in fact favour him. Virgil is deliberately putting a confident battlefield proverb into the mouth of the man about to be destroyed.

Detached from that context, the saying became one of the most durable mottoes in the Western world — adopted by military units, universities, and clubs, and endlessly requoted as plain encouragement to take risks. The version that circulates is the proverb, not the tragic scene.
detailsBody: Ennius, Annals 257: fortibus est fortuna viris data (“fortune is given to brave men”).
Terence, Phormio 203: fortis Fortuna adiuvat (“fortune helps the brave”).
Pliny the Younger reports his uncle, Pliny the Elder, saying fortes fortuna iuvat as he sailed toward the erupting Vesuvius in AD 79.
